# §10 — Positioning: our numbers beside published ones

*Table generated by `python3 paper/make_positioning_table.py` from `results/` and
`paper/external_numbers.json`. Our cells are computed from committed artifacts;
published cells carry the verbatim sentence they came from, and any value that
reached us second-hand is held back rather than rendered.*

§4 answers a reviewer who asks *what did you compare against?* — an undefended
floor and a published prompt-level defense, both re-implemented and run inside
our own pipeline on our own corpus. This section answers the different question
underneath it: *how do your numbers sit against the numbers other people
published?*

The two are not the same question, and the second one is mostly a trap. Every
published figure below was measured on a different corpus, with a different
agent, against a different threat model, and scored by a different metric. Not
one of them is a like-for-like comparison with ours, and we do not present any of
them as one. What the table is for is calibration: it shows where our numbers sit
in the range the field reports, which of our numbers are unremarkable, and the
one place where our result genuinely diverges from what a reader would expect.

Three rules govern every row:

1. **No pooled cell.** InjecAgent is reported per stratum here for the same
   reason it is in §5 — the two strata are drawn 30/30 from a 51/459 population,
   so a pooled figure is wrong by 33 points.
2. **The published column is quoted, not recalled.** Each entry in
   `external_numbers.json` carries the sentence or table cell it came from. A row
   with no quote does not render.
3. **Our ablations never appear as baselines.** `static_only` is labelled as ours
   everywhere it occurs.

### A. Attack success, on a corpus somebody else built

*Ours: `results/phase12/benchmark.json`, InjecAgent `direct_harm_base`, n = 60 drawn 30/30 across the two strata. Published: [Zhan et al.](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.624/), InjecAgent, 1,054 test cases, 17 user tools, 62 attacker instructions.*

| System | Setting | ASR | Why it is not a like-for-like |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **AdaptiShield, undefended** | gemma3:4b / qwen2.5:3b | **100.0%** 60/60 [94.0, 100.0] | our undefended floor, same corpus |
| **AdaptiShield, `static_only`** | same | **100.0%** 60/60 [94.0, 100.0] | the rule layer alone stops nothing here |
| ReAct-prompted GPT-4 (undefended) | base | 24.0% | ASR-valid over all attack types, not direct-harm only; no interval reported |
| ReAct-prompted GPT-4 (undefended) | enhanced (hacking prompt prepended) | 47.0% | ASR-valid over all attack types, not direct-harm only; no interval reported |
| ReAct-prompted Llama2-70B (undefended) | both settings, lower bound | >80% | ASR-valid over all attack types, not direct-harm only; no interval reported |
| Fine-tuned GPT-4 / GPT-3.5 (undefended) | base; GPT-3.5 is 6.6% | 3.8% | ASR-valid over all attack types, not direct-harm only; no interval reported |

**Read this as a floor check, not a win.** Our 100% is the *undefended* number, and it sits above every model InjecAgent reports because our agent is a 3–4B local model, not GPT-4. That is the point of the row: the attacks land on our harness, so a downstream difference means something. It is not evidence that our setting is harder in any interesting way.

### B. Detection, against published detectors

*Ours: `results/noise_floor/{injecagent,agentdojo_benign}.json`, median of 3 repeats, per stratum and never pooled. Published: [Zou et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14005), averages over OPI, Dolly, MMLU, BoolQ (short context) and Musique, NarrativeQA (long context); FPR on clean splits, FNR on injected splits.*

| Detector | Detection (1 − FNR) | FPR | Evaluated on |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **AdaptiShield 3B — target-bearing stratum** | **96.7%** 29/30 [83.3, 99.4] | **3.3%** 2/60 [0.9, 11.4] | InjecAgent direct-harm / AgentDojo benign |
| **AdaptiShield 3B — no-target stratum** | **10.0%** 3/30 [3.5, 25.6] | **3.3%** 2/60 [0.9, 11.4] | same |
| PIShield | 98.6% | 0.5% | text benchmarks, no agent loop |
| PIGuard | 29.8% | 0.7% | text benchmarks, no agent loop |
| PromptArmor | 54.1% | 1.3% | text benchmarks, no agent loop |
| InjecGuard | 33.7% | 8.2% | text benchmarks, no agent loop |
| ProtectAI-deberta | 24.1% | 10.1% | text benchmarks, no agent loop |
| TaskTracker | 68.3% | 27.4% | text benchmarks, no agent loop |
| AttentionTracker | 44.7% | 32.8% | text benchmarks, no agent loop |
| DataSentinel | 89.6% | 33.6% | text benchmarks, no agent loop |
| PromptGuard | 91.3% | 40.3% | text benchmarks, no agent loop |

Repeat spread: target 29–29/30 across 3 repeats, no-target 3–4/30 across 3 repeats, false positives 2–2/60 across 3 repeats.

**The comparison is indicative and the direction of the bias is known.** Those detectors classify a *text* prompt on short- and long-context QA corpora; ours classifies a *turn of an agent loop* on injected tool output, and its input is the causal contrast rather than the raw text. Neither number transfers. What does transfer is the shape: published detectors trade FPR against FNR along one axis, and ours splits along a different one — near-ceiling where the injection carries a liftable target, near-floor where it does not, at one fixed false-positive rate.

### C. The published prompt-level defense, re-measured

*Ours: `results/phase10/benchmark.json`, 66 malicious pairs, `steer_rate`. Published: [Hines et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14720).*

| Measurement | Before | After | Test |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Spotlighting, our harness** | **34.8%** 23/66 [24.5, 46.9] | **33.3%** 22/66 [23.2, 45.3] | paired McNemar **p = 1.00**, 8 helped / 7 hurt |
| Spotlighting, as published | >50% | <2% | from >50% to <2%, GPT-family; no interval or paired test reported |

| Other published defense | Result | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Tool filter defense (GPT-4o — stated in the body text, not read off Table 5) | targeted attack success rate **7.5%** | [Debenedetti et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352) |
| No defense, important-instructions attack (GPT-4o, 95% CI ±3.9) | targeted attack success rate **57.7%** | [Debenedetti et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352) |
| Delimiting defense (prompt-level) (GPT-4o, 95% CI ±3.9) | targeted attack success rate **41.6%** | [Debenedetti et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352) |

**We do not claim spotlighting does not work.** We claim it had no measurable effect *here* — 3–4B local models, our corpus, action selection as the outcome — and we report the paired test rather than two overlapping intervals. The gap between >50% → <2% and 34.8% → 33.3% is most likely a gap in setting, and §4 gives the decomposition that makes the null informative rather than empty.

## What the table is actually evidence for

Read down the detection block and the field's numbers form a familiar trade:
detectors sit somewhere on an FPR/FNR curve, and a paper's contribution is
usually a better point on it. Our detector does not sit on that curve at all. At
one fixed false-positive rate it is near the ceiling on one stratum and near the
floor on the other, and the split is not a threshold artifact — it is the
presence or absence of a liftable target in the injected text, the same quantity
Phase 15 measured directly.

That is the paper's spine restated in somebody else's units. It also says
something about how the field reports detection: none of the published detectors
we found reports its numbers stratified this way, so a mechanism-dependent
collapse of this size would not be visible in any of their tables. We are not
claiming those systems share the failure. We are claiming their evaluations, as
reported, could not tell us either way — and that is a related-work observation
with an experiment behind it rather than a rhetorical one.

## What we could not position

- **The campaign detection headline.** 96.7% on an attack set we wrote is not
  comparable with any published number, and it is the one figure in the paper
  without a committed artifact. Both facts are stated in the table rather than
  worked around.
- **AgentDojo's undefended attack success rate.** We have the tool-filter figure
  verbatim; the no-defense baseline reached us second-hand and is held back by
  the generator until someone reads the table in the paper itself.
- **Utility.** Every agent-benchmark paper here reports utility under attack, and
  we report `steer_rate` and workflow-continuation instead. Our corpus has no
  benign task-completion metric of comparable construction, so there is no honest
  row to write. §9 carries this as a limitation.
